verifiedClaims.claim: A driver who was speeding, texting, or otherwise negligent is still liable even if the pedestrian was intoxicated.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The driver's negligence remains actionable, but the pedestrian's recovery is reduced by his or her share of fault and barred entirely at 50% or more in Georgia (§ 51-12-33(g)) or 51% or more in South Carolina. Politzer v. Xiaoyan, 342 Ga. App. 224, 801 S.E.2d 114 (2017), cert. denied (as annotated under §§ 40-6-91 and 40-6-95): summary judgment for the driver affirmed where the drunk pedestrian, in black clothing, crossed a major road at night outside an available crosswalk and there was no evidence the driver was speeding, violating any rule of the road, or even saw him.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Politzer v. Xiaoyan (Ga. Ct. App. 2017), annotation to O.C.G.A. § 40-6-95 (Justia)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Is still liable' overstates: liability turns on the fault split. Reword: 'A driver who was speeding, texting, or otherwise negligent can still be held liable even if the pedestrian was intoxicated — the pedestrian's share of fault reduces the award rather than erasing the claim, unless it reaches the state's bar.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Missing these deadlines means losing your right to sue.
verifiedClaims.note: General statement; tolling exceptions (e.g., minors, S.C. Code § 15-3-40 capped at one year after disability ends) exist but need not be listed in an FAQ.

verifiedClaims.claim: but they cannot legally deny it solely because you were drinking
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No statute in either state forbids a liability insurer from denying a third-party bodily-injury claim. The unfair-claims-practices statutes (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34; S.C. Code § 38-59-20) are enforced by the insurance regulator, Georgia's bad-faith penalty (§ 33-4-6) runs only to the policyholder, and South Carolina 'does not recognize a third party action for bad faith refusal to pay insurance benefits' (Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)). What is true is that intoxication alone does not bar recovery under either state's comparative-fault rule, so a denial on that ground can be tested by suing the driver.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co. (S.C. 2000); O.C.G.A. §§ 33-4-6, 33-6-34; S.C. Code § 38-59-20 (verified in facts-1679/1709/1744)
verifiedClaims.note: Reword: 'Insurance companies will try to use your intoxication to minimize or deny your claim, but drinking alone does not bar recovery in either state — if the driver was negligent, a denial can be challenged by filing suit against the driver.' Published as FAQPage schema, so fix in meta.

verifiedClaims.claim: Admissible to show contributory negligence
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia and South Carolina both apply comparative (not contributory) negligence; evidence of a pedestrian's intoxication is relevant to his or her share of fault. Both states also make it an offense for a pedestrian under the influence 'to a degree which renders him a hazard' to be on the roadway: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-95 ('shall not walk or be upon any roadway or the shoulder of any roadway'; misdemeanor, fine up to $500) and S.C. Code § 56-5-3270 ('shall not walk or be upon a highway except a sidewalk'). The defense must prove the 'hazard' degree: in Swinney v. Schneider Nat'l Carriers, 829 F. Supp. 2d 1358 (N.D. Ga. 2011), defendants failed to show as a matter of law that alcohol and cocaine in the decedent's system rendered him a 'hazard' under § 40-6-95.

South Carolina: capped at the greater of three times compensatory or $500,000 (CPI-indexed; $739,245 for 2026 per RFA, facts-1663), but uncapped against an impaired defendant (§ 15-32-530(C)(3)).

verifiedClaims.note: Fine as an investigation item. Do not extend it into a claim that the citation proves negligence at trial.

recommendedEdits: Body, Georgia driver duties: change 'Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-91, drivers must exercise due care to avoid striking any pedestrian on a roadway and must give warning by sounding the horn when necessary.' to 'Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93, drivers must exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian on a roadway, must give warning by sounding the horn when necessary, and must exercise proper precautions upon observing any child or any obviously confused, incapacitated, or intoxicated person.'

Body, Georgia driver duties: change 'Drivers must also yield to pedestrians in marked or unmarked crosswalks at intersections.' to 'Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-91, drivers must also stop and remain stopped for a pedestrian within a crosswalk who is on their half of the road or within one lane of it.'

Body, Georgia pedestrian duties: append to the § 40-6-92 sentence ', unless the pedestrian has already, and under safe conditions, entered the roadway'. Then add: 'Georgia also makes it a misdemeanor for a person under the influence of alcohol or drugs to a degree which renders him a hazard to walk or be upon any roadway or its shoulder (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-95), and insurers will cite it. But it is not automatic: the defense must prove the pedestrian was impaired to the point of being a hazard. And the claim still depends on proof of driver fault: in Politzer v. Xiaoyan (Ga. Ct. App. 2017), the court ruled for the driver without trial where the drunk pedestrian crossed a dark road outside a crosswalk and there was no evidence the driver was speeding or broke any traffic rule.'

Body, SC driver duties: change '§ 56-5-3130' to '§ 56-5-3230' and replace 'any child or any confused or incapacitated person on the roadway.' with 'any child or any obviously confused, incapacitated or intoxicated person.' Replace 'This "incapacitated person" language can apply to visibly intoxicated pedestrians, imposing a heightened duty of care on drivers.' with 'The statute names intoxicated persons expressly, so a driver who sees a pedestrian staggering or disoriented must take extra care. Georgia's due-care statute uses nearly identical words (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93).'

Body, SC intro: replace 'South Carolina courts have recognized that a driver's duty to exercise care toward pedestrians is not diminished by the pedestrian's intoxication.' with 'South Carolina's due-care statute expressly requires drivers to exercise proper precaution upon observing any obviously intoxicated person (S.C. Code § 56-5-3230).' Add '(Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 1991)' after the 51% sentence.

Body, SC pedestrian duties: replace with 'S.C. Code § 56-5-3150 requires pedestrians crossing anywhere other than a marked crosswalk or an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection to yield the right-of-way to vehicles, and § 56-5-3270 bars a pedestrian impaired to the point of being a hazard from being on a highway except a sidewalk.'

Comparison table: change both 'Admissible to show contributory negligence' cells to 'Relevant to your share of fault' (GA cell may add '(O.C.G.A. § 40-6-95)'; SC cell '(S.C. Code § 56-5-3270)'). Add '(Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.)' to the SC 'Must be less than 51% at fault' cell.

Body, driver-duties list lead-in: change 'Courts in both states have held that the following driver behaviors can establish negligence even when the pedestrian was impaired:' to 'Evidence of any of the following driver conduct can establish negligence even when the pedestrian was impaired:'. Optional sentence after the list: 'Georgia's Supreme Court has held that even a person lying drunk in the road is owed a duty of care, and a driver must keep a lookout to discover that person's peril (Fountain v. Thompson, 252 Ga. 256 (1984)).'
Body, intro: change 'Cornell Law Institute's overview of comparative negligence' to 'the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School's overview of comparative negligence' (keep href).
Optional body, punitive sentence: append 'and when the driver was impaired, neither state caps them (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f); S.C. Code § 15-32-530(C)(3)).'

Optional body, SOL subsections: add one sentence on government defendants — South Carolina Tort Claims Act two years, or three if a verified claim is filed first (S.C. Code § 15-78-110); Georgia ante litem notice deadlines for cities (6 months, § 36-33-5), counties (12 months, § 36-11-1) and the state (12 months, § 50-21-26).

Optional statistic (the post has none; only if the editor wants one, e.g. in the intro): 'According to NHTSA, an estimated 30 percent of pedestrians killed in U.S. traffic crashes in 2023 had a blood alcohol concentration of .08 g/dL or higher, and alcohol involvement — for the driver and/or the pedestrian — was reported in 46 percent of fatal pedestrian crashes.'
